Siyang Ni

2025-11-13

user-manual.Rmd

Introduction

About This Manual

This comprehensive manual covers all aspects of the surveymixr package, from basic concepts to advanced applications. It consolidates information from all package vignettes into a single, unified guide suitable for both beginners and advanced users.

What is surveymixr?

surveymixr is the first R package to implement growth mixture modeling (GMM) with full integration of complex survey design features. It enables rigorous analysis of longitudinal data from large-scale surveys (e.g., Millennium Cohort Study, Add Health, NLSY, ECLS) that were previously only possible in proprietary software like Mplus.

Key Features

  • Complex Survey Integration: Full support for stratification, clustering (PSUs), and probability weights
  • Survey-Adjusted Standard Errors: Sandwich estimators accounting for design effects
  • Multiple Outcome Types: Continuous, binary, ordinal, and count outcomes
  • Advanced Model Selection: Bootstrap LRT (BLRT), Lo-Mendell-Rubin test, cross-validation
  • R3STEP Method: Classification uncertainty correction for auxiliary variables
  • Random Effects: Individual-level variance in growth parameters
  • Time-Varying Covariates: Within-person and between-person effects
  • Comprehensive Diagnostics: Convergence tracking, influence detection, separation checks
  • Professional Visualization: Publication-ready plots with ggplot2 and plotly
  • Parallel Processing: Efficient handling of 500-1000+ random starts

Why Choose surveymixr?

Part I: Getting Started

Installation

From CRAN (Recommended) 

install.packages("surveymixr")

Development Version from GitHub 

# Install devtools if needed
install.packages("devtools")

# Install surveymixr
devtools::install_github("siyangni/surveymixr")

System Requirements

  • R (>= 4.0.0)
  • No compiled code (pure R package, works on all platforms)

Loading the Package 

library(surveymixr)

# Check version
packageVersion("surveymixr")

Quick Start Example

Load Example Data 

# Load simulated Millennium Cohort Study data
data(mcs_simulated)

# Examine data structure
head(mcs_simulated)
str(mcs_simulated)

The data contains: - id: Individual identifier - age: Time points (3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 17 years) - selfcontrol: Outcome variable (self-control scores) - stratum, psu, weight: Survey design variables - true_class: True class membership (for validation)

Fit a Basic 3-Class Model 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  growth_model = "linear",
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 100,
  cores = 4,
  verbose = TRUE
)

View Results 

# Comprehensive summary
summary(fit)

# Extract fit indices
extract_fit_indices(fit)

# Classification quality
classification_quality(fit)

Visualize Trajectories 

# Static plot
plot(fit, type = "trajectories")

# Interactive plot
plot_interactive(fit, type = "trajectories")

Part II: Core Concepts

Growth Mixture Models

What are GMMs?

Growth mixture models (GMMs) identify subgroups with distinct developmental trajectories in longitudinal data. They combine:

  1. Growth Models: Model change over time within individuals
  2. Mixture Models: Identify latent subgroups (classes) with different patterns
  3. Survey Design: Account for complex sampling structures

When to Use GMMs

Use GMMs when: - You have longitudinal data (3+ time points) - You suspect heterogeneity in trajectories - You want to identify distinct developmental patterns - Data comes from complex surveys with sampling weights

Model Components 

Y_it = f(time) + ε_it        # Within-class growth model
P(Class = k) = π_k           # Class membership probabilities

Where: - Y_it: Outcome for individual i at time t - f(time): Growth function (linear, quadratic, etc.) - ε_it: Residual error - π_k: Proportion in class k

Complex Survey Design

Why Survey Design Matters

Ignoring survey design features leads to: - Biased standard errors (usually underestimated) - Invalid p-values and confidence intervals - Incorrect inference about class differences

Survey Features in surveymixr

1. Stratification - Divides population into non-overlapping groups - Example: Geographic regions, urban/rural

2. Clustering (PSUs) - Individuals sampled in groups - Example: Schools, neighborhoods - Creates within-cluster correlation

3. Probability Weights - Adjust for unequal sampling probabilities - Example: Oversampling of minorities - Ensures nationally representative estimates

4. Survey-Adjusted Standard Errors - Uses sandwich estimator - Accounts for design effects - Produces valid inference

Specifying Survey Design 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  outcome = "outcome",
  n_classes = 3,

  # Survey design features:
  strata = "stratum_var",     # Stratification variable
  cluster = "psu_var",        # Primary sampling unit
  weights = "weight_var",     # Sampling weights
  nest = TRUE                 # PSUs nested within strata
)

Part III: Basic Model Fitting

Model Specification

Required Arguments 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = your_data,           # Long-format data frame
  id = "id_variable",         # Individual ID
  time = "time_variable",     # Time variable
  outcome = "outcome_var",    # Outcome variable
  n_classes = 3               # Number of latent classes
)

Growth Model Types

1. Linear Growth (Default)

fit <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "linear")
# Y_it = β0 + β1*time + ε

2. Quadratic Growth

fit <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "quadratic")
# Y_it = β0 + β1*time + β2*time² + ε

3. Nonlinear Growth

fit <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "nonlinear")
# Flexible spline-based trajectories

4. Free Basis (Time Scores)

fit <- gmm_survey(..., growth_model = "free_basis")
# Estimates time loadings freely

Estimation Options 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  ...,
  starts = 500,              # Number of random starts (higher = better)
  convergence = 1e-6,        # Convergence criterion
  max_iter = 1000,           # Maximum EM iterations
  cores = 4,                 # Parallel processing cores
  keep_data = TRUE,          # Store data in object (for diagnostics)
  verbose = TRUE             # Print progress
)

Recommended Settings: - starts: 200-500 for exploration, 500-1000 for final models - cores: Set to number of available CPU cores - convergence: Default (1e-6) is usually adequate

Examining Results

Summary Output 

summary(fit)

Shows: - Model information (classes, growth model, sample size) - Survey design features - Fit indices (AIC, BIC, aBIC, entropy, log-likelihood) - Class proportions (weighted and unweighted) - Growth parameters by class - Standard errors

Extracting Components 

# Coefficients
coef(fit)

# Variance-covariance matrix
vcov(fit)

# Log-likelihood
logLik(fit)

# Information criteria
AIC(fit)
BIC(fit)

# Fit indices table
extract_fit_indices(fit)

# Predicted trajectories
trajectories <- extract_trajectories(fit, class = 1)

Classification 

# Posterior probabilities
post_probs <- fit@posterior_probs
head(post_probs)

# Most likely class assignments
class_assignments <- fit@class_assignments
table(class_assignments)

# Classification quality
classification_quality(fit)

# Entropy (higher = better separation)
entropy(fit)

# Class proportions
class_proportions(fit)

Part IV: Model Selection

Determining the Number of Classes

Model selection is critical in GMM. Use multiple criteria:

1. Information Criteria

Lower is better for IC measures:

# Compare models with different class counts
selection <- gmm_select(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  classes = 1:5,              # Test 1-5 classes
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  criteria = c("BIC", "aBIC", "entropy"),
  starts = 200,
  cores = 4
)

# View results
print(selection)
plot_model_selection(selection)

Criteria: - BIC: Bayesian Information Criterion (most commonly used) - aBIC: Sample-size adjusted BIC (for large samples) - AIC: Akaike Information Criterion (less penalized)

Decision Rule: - Choose model where IC reaches minimum or “elbow” - Lower values indicate better fit - Balance fit vs. parsimony

2. Bootstrap Likelihood Ratio Test (BLRT)

Gold standard for class enumeration:

selection <- gmm_select(
  ...,
  criteria = c("BIC", "BLRT"),
  blrt_samples = 100,        # Bootstrap samples
  blrt_cores = 4             # Parallel processing
)

Interpretation: - Tests k-class vs. (k-1)-class model - Significant p-value → k-class model is better - Stop when p-value becomes non-significant

3. Lo-Mendell-Rubin (LMR) Test

Faster alternative to BLRT (no bootstrap):

# Fit two models
fit2 <- gmm_survey(..., n_classes = 2, ...)
fit3 <- gmm_survey(..., n_classes = 3, ...)

# LMR test
lmr_result <- lmr_test(fit3, fit2, adjusted = TRUE)
print(lmr_result)

Advantages: - Much faster than BLRT - Good approximation in large samples

Disadvantages: - Less accurate in small samples - May be anti-conservative

4. Cross-Validation

Predictive performance approach:

cv_results <- gmm_cv(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  classes = 1:5,
  k_folds = 5,              # 5-fold CV
  stratified = TRUE,         # Maintain class proportions
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 100,
  cores = 4
)

print(cv_results)
plot(cv_results)

Metrics: - Predictive log-likelihood - Mean squared prediction error (MSPE) - One-standard-error rule

5. Classification Quality 

# For each candidate model
classification_quality(fit)

Metrics: - Entropy (0-1): Higher = better separation (>0.80 good) - AvePP (Average Posterior Probability): >0.70 adequate, >0.80 good - OCC (Odds of Correct Classification): >5 adequate

Recommended Strategy

  1. Start with IC (BIC, aBIC) to narrow range
  2. Use BLRT to confirm optimal k
  3. Check classification quality (entropy, AvePP)
  4. Consider interpretability and theoretical fit
  5. Validate with CV if computational resources allow

Example Workflow:

# Step 1: Comprehensive selection
selection <- gmm_select(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",
  classes = 1:6,
  strata = "stratum", cluster = "psu", weights = "weight",
  criteria = c("BIC", "aBIC", "entropy", "BLRT"),
  blrt_samples = 100,
  starts = 500,
  cores = 4
)

print(selection)
plot_model_selection(selection)

# Step 2: Fit final model
best_k <- selection@recommended_classes$BLRT
fit_final <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = best_k,
  strata = "stratum", cluster = "psu", weights = "weight",
  starts = 1000,  # More starts for final model
  cores = 4
)

# Step 3: Validate
diagnose_convergence(fit_final)
classification_quality(fit_final)

Part V: Outcome Types

Continuous Outcomes (Default) 

fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "continuous_var",
  n_classes = 3,
  outcome_type = "continuous"  # Default
)

Assumptions: - Normal distribution - Linear relationship (or specify quadratic/nonlinear)

Binary Outcomes 

fit_binary <- gmm_survey_binary(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "binary_var",  # 0/1
  n_classes = 3,
  link = "probit",           # or "logit"
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight"
)

Link Functions: - "probit" (default): Assumes normal latent variable - "logit": Logistic model

Example: Smoking initiation trajectories (yes/no)

Ordinal Outcomes 

fit_ordinal <- gmm_survey_ordinal(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "ordinal_var",  # 1,2,3,4,5
  n_classes = 3,
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight"
)

Model: - Proportional odds model - Ordered categories (e.g., Likert scales)

Example: Health rating trajectories (Poor, Fair, Good, Very Good, Excellent)

Count Outcomes 

fit_count <- gmm_survey_count(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "count_var",  # 0,1,2,3,...
  n_classes = 3,
  distribution = "poisson",  # or "negbin", "zip"
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight"
)

Distributions: - "poisson": Simple count model - "negbin": Negative binomial (handles overdispersion) - "zip": Zero-inflated Poisson (excess zeros)

Example: Delinquency trajectories (number of incidents)

Part VI: Advanced Features

Random Effects Models

Why Random Effects?

Standard GMM assumes no within-class variance in growth parameters. Random effects add:

  • Individual-level deviations from class means
  • More realistic modeling of heterogeneity
  • Better fit for highly variable trajectories

Fitting RE Models 

fit_re <- gmm_survey_re(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  random = ~ 1 + age,        # Random intercept and slope
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  starts = 200,
  cores = 4
)

Extracting Random Effects 

# Get BLUPs (Best Linear Unbiased Predictors)
random_effects <- get_random_effects(fit_re)
head(random_effects)

# Variance components
variance_components(fit_re)

# Intraclass correlations
calculate_icc(fit_re)

# Visualize
plot_random_effects(fit_re, type = "density")
plot_random_effects(fit_re, type = "caterpillar")

Time-Varying Covariates

Why TVCs?

Model how within-person changes in predictors affect outcomes.

Example: How does stress (changing over time) affect mental health trajectories?

Fitting TVC Models 

fit_tvc <- gmm_survey_tvc(
  data = your_data,
  id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "outcome",
  n_classes = 3,
  tvc_formula = ~ stress + support,  # Time-varying predictors
  tvc_effect = "both",               # Within + between effects
  lag = 1,                           # Lagged effects
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight"
)

Effect Types: - "direct": Contemporaneous effects - "indirect": Mediated through growth - "both": Within-person + between-person decomposition - "interaction": TVC × time interaction

Interpreting TVC Results 

# Extract effects
tvc_effects <- extract_tvc_effects(fit_tvc)
print(tvc_effects)

# Statistical tests
test_tvc_effects(fit_tvc)

# Visualize
plot_tvc_effects(fit_tvc, covariate = "stress")

Part VII: Auxiliary Variable Analysis

The R3STEP Approach

Why R3STEP?

Problem: Direct inclusion of auxiliary variables (e.g., demographics, outcomes) in GMM can: - Alter class formation - Lead to biased estimates - Change class membership

Solution: R3STEP performs auxiliary analysis after class formation, accounting for classification uncertainty.

When to Use R3STEP

Use R3STEP to: - Compare classes on distal outcomes (e.g., academic achievement) - Examine demographic differences between classes - Test predictors of class membership - Avoid bias from classification error

Fitting R3STEP Models 

# Step 1: Fit GMM (without auxiliary variables)
fit <- gmm_survey(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id", time = "age", outcome = "selfcontrol",
  n_classes = 3,
  strata = "stratum", cluster = "psu", weights = "weight",
  starts = 500
)

# Step 2: Prepare distal variables (one row per individual)
distal_data <- mcs_simulated[!duplicated(mcs_simulated$id), ]

# Step 3: R3STEP analysis
r3step_results <- r3step(
  gmm_object = fit,
  distal_vars = c("academic_achievement", "delinquency", "ses"),
  data = distal_data,
  method = "BCH"             # or "ML", "manual"
)

Methods

1. BCH (Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars) - Default method - Most commonly used - Good balance of bias and efficiency

2. ML (Maximum Likelihood) - More efficient - Slightly more complex

3. Manual (Three-Step) - Simple but potentially biased - Use for comparison only

Interpreting R3STEP Results 

# Comprehensive summary
summary(r3step_results)

# Class-specific means for distal variables
print(r3step_results@class_means)

# Omnibus tests (overall differences across classes)
print(r3step_results@test_results)

# Effect sizes (Cohen's d for pairwise comparisons)
print(r3step_results@effect_sizes)

Interpretation: - Omnibus test: Are there overall differences? - Pairwise tests: Which classes differ? - Effect sizes: How large are differences? (d > 0.5 = medium, d > 0.8 = large)

Part VIII: Diagnostics

Convergence Diagnostics

Why Check Convergence?

GMM estimation can find local maxima. Multiple random starts help find the global maximum.

Diagnose Convergence 

conv_diag <- diagnose_convergence(fit)
print(conv_diag)

# Visualize distribution of log-likelihoods
plot(conv_diag)

Red Flags: - ⚠️ Best solution replicated <10% of the time - ⚠️ Multiple distinct local maxima - ⚠️ Wide range of log-likelihood values

Solutions: - Increase starts (e.g., 500 → 1000) - Try different initialization methods - Consider simpler model (fewer classes)

Influence Diagnostics

Detecting Influential Cases 

# Requires keep_data = TRUE in original fit
fit <- gmm_survey(..., keep_data = TRUE)

# Influence diagnostics
influence <- diagnose_influence(fit, measure = "all")
print(influence)

# Get influential IDs
influential_ids <- influence@influential_ids

# Examine influential cases
mcs_simulated[mcs_simulated$id %in% influential_ids, ]

Measures: - Cook’s Distance: Overall influence on parameters - DFBETAS: Parameter-specific influence - Leverage: Unusual predictor patterns

Actions: - Examine influential cases for data quality issues - Sensitivity analysis: Refit without influential cases - Consider robustness checks

Separation Diagnostics

Detecting Perfect Separation 

sep_diag <- diagnose_separation(fit)
print(sep_diag)

Problems: - Perfect separation: Classes completely distinct - Quasi-separation: Near-perfect distinction - Empty classes: Class with 0 or very few members

Solutions: - Reduce number of classes - Check for data issues or outliers - Add constraints

Residual Diagnostics 

resid_diag <- residual_diagnostics(fit)
print(resid_diag)

Checks: - Normality (Shapiro-Wilk test, Q-Q plots) - Outliers - Autocorrelation - Class-specific patterns

Part X: Data Management

Data Validation

Pre-Analysis Checks 

validation <- validate_survey_data(
  data = mcs_simulated,
  id = "id",
  time = "age",
  outcome = "selfcontrol",
  strata = "stratum",
  cluster = "psu",
  weights = "weight",
  min_observations = 3,     # Minimum time points per person
  check_weights = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE
)

print(validation)

Checks: - Data structure (duplicates, missing values) - Survey design validity (nested clusters, weights) - Missing data patterns - Outcome distribution - Covariate multicollinearity

Actions: - Review validation@errors for critical issues - Consider validation@warnings for potential problems - Follow validation@recommendations

Data Preparation

Wide to Long Format 

# Wide format data
wide_data <- data.frame(
  id = 1:100,
  y_t1 = rnorm(100),
  y_t2 = rnorm(100),
  y_t3 = rnorm(100)
)

# Convert to long
long_data <- wide_to_long(
  data = wide_data,
  id_var = "id",
  outcome_vars = c("y_t1", "y_t2", "y_t3"),
  time_values = c(0, 1, 2)
)

Missing Data

surveymixr uses Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) by default: - Handles missing data automatically - No need for imputation - Valid under MAR (Missing At Random) assumption

Patterns:

# Check missing patterns in validation
validation@info$missing_patterns

Part XI: Software Integration

Integration with Mplus

Convert Mplus Syntax to R 

# Read Mplus .inp file
r_code <- mplus_to_surveymixr("my_analysis.inp")

# View suggested R code
cat(r_code)

Generate Mplus-Style Output 

# Create Mplus-formatted output
surveymixr_to_mplus(fit, file = "surveymixr_results.txt")

Validate Against Mplus 

# Compare results (manual)
compare_with_mplus(fit, "mplus_output.out")

Typical Differences: - Minor numerical differences due to optimization algorithms - surveymixr may find better solutions with more random starts - Standard errors should be very similar

Part XII: Simulation & Testing

Simulate Data

Basic Simulation 

sim_data <- simulate_gmm_survey(
  n_individuals = 1000,
  n_times = 5,
  n_classes = 3,
  time_scores = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4),

  # Growth parameters by class
  class_params = list(
    class1 = list(intercept = 50, slope = 2),
    class2 = list(intercept = 40, slope = 0),
    class3 = list(intercept = 60, slope = -1)
  ),

  # Class proportions
  class_proportions = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3),

  # Survey design
  design = "stratified_cluster",
  n_strata = 4,
  n_clusters = 50,

  # Missing data
  missing_rate = 0.15,

  seed = 123
)

Power Analysis 

# Simulate multiple datasets to assess power
results <- replicate(100, {
  sim <- simulate_gmm_survey(...)
  fit <- gmm_survey(sim, ...)
  classification_quality(fit)$entropy
}, simplify = FALSE)

# Analyze power
mean(sapply(results, function(x) x > 0.80))

Part XIII: Best Practices

Workflow Recommendations

1. Exploratory Phase 

# Quick exploration with fewer starts
fit_explore <- gmm_survey(
  ...,
  starts = 100,
  cores = 4
)

2. Model Selection Phase 

# Comprehensive comparison
selection <- gmm_select(
  ...,
  classes = 1:6,
  criteria = c("BIC", "BLRT", "entropy"),
  blrt_samples = 100,
  starts = 200,
  cores = 4
)

3. Final Model Phase 

# Best model with more starts
fit_final <- gmm_survey(
  ...,
  n_classes = best_k,
  starts = 1000,
  cores = 4,
  keep_data = TRUE
)

# Thorough diagnostics
diagnose_convergence(fit_final)
diagnose_influence(fit_final)
classification_quality(fit_final)

Reporting Results

Essential Information

Include in publications: 1. Model specification: Classes, growth model, covariates 2. Sample: N, time points, missing data handling 3. Survey design: Strata, clusters, weights 4. Estimation: Random starts, convergence 5. Model selection: Criteria used, comparison table 6. Classification quality: Entropy, AvePP 7. Parameters: Growth parameters with SEs 8. Diagnostics: Convergence checks

Example Results Table 

# Create comparison table
comparison <- data.frame(
  Classes = 1:5,
  LogLik = sapply(model_list, logLik),
  AIC = sapply(model_list, AIC),
  BIC = sapply(model_list, BIC),
  Entropy = sapply(model_list, function(m) entropy(m))
)

print(comparison)

Computational Efficiency

Parallel Processing 

# Use all available cores
fit <- gmm_survey(
  ...,
  cores = parallel::detectCores() - 1  # Leave 1 for system
)

Memory Management 

# Don't store data unless needed
fit <- gmm_survey(..., keep_data = FALSE)

# Clear old models
rm(fit_old)
gc()

Part XIV: Troubleshooting

Common Issues

1. Convergence Failures

Problem: “Model did not converge”

Solutions: - Increase max_iter (e.g., 1000 → 2000) - Increase starts (e.g., 200 → 500) - Try simpler model (fewer classes) - Check for data issues (outliers, missing)

2. Separation Warnings

Problem: “Classes are perfectly separated”

Solutions: - Reduce number of classes - Check for extreme values or data errors - Consider different growth model - Add constraints on parameters

3. Local Maxima

Problem: Best solution replicated infrequently

Solutions: - Increase random starts - Use different initialization - Try multiple runs and compare

4. Negative Variance Estimates

Problem: “Negative variance detected”

Solutions: - Fix variance to positive value - Constrain variances across classes - Check model identification

5. Slow Performance

Problem: Estimation takes too long

Solutions: - Reduce starts for initial exploration - Use more cores for parallelization - Start with simpler model - Consider smaller subset for testing

Error Messages

Data-Related Errors 

Error: ID variable not found

→ Check spelling of id parameter

Error: Duplicate id-time combinations

→ Data has repeated observations; fix data structure

Estimation Errors 

Error: Numerical instability

→ Try rescaling outcome variable (z-score)

Warning: Hessian is not positive definite

→ Model may be misspecified or unidentified

Part XV: Advanced Topics

Custom Growth Models

Piecewise Linear Growth 

# Create piecewise time variable
data$time1 <- ifelse(data$time <= 5, data$time, 5)
data$time2 <- ifelse(data$time > 5, data$time - 5, 0)

# Fit model with both slopes
# (requires manual specification)

Cohort Effects 

# Include cohort as time-invariant predictor in R3STEP
r3step_results <- r3step(
  gmm_object = fit,
  distal_vars = c("cohort", "other_outcomes"),
  data = distal_data
)

Multiple Group Analysis

By Gender 

# Fit separate models
fit_male <- gmm_survey(data_male, ...)
fit_female <- gmm_survey(data_female, ...)

# Compare class structures
compare_classes(fit_male, fit_female)

Appendix B: Formulas & Mathematics

EM Algorithm

surveymixr uses the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm:

E-Step: Compute posterior probabilities P(Ci=k|Yi)=πkf(Yi|θk)∑j=1Kπjf(Yi|θj)P(C_i = k | Y_i) = \frac{\pi_k f(Y_i | \theta_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j f(Y_i | \theta_j)}

M-Step: Update parameters θ(t+1)=argmaxθ∑i=1N∑k=1KP(Ci=k|Yi;θ(t))logf(Yi|θk)\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K P(C_i=k|Y_i;\theta^{(t)}) \log f(Y_i|\theta_k)

Survey-Adjusted Standard Errors

Sandwich estimator: Var(θ̂)=H−1ΣH−1\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = H^{-1} \Sigma H^{-1}

Where: - HH = Hessian matrix - Σ\Sigma = Survey-adjusted score covariance

Information Criteria

AIC=−2logL+2p\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2pBIC=−2logL+plogN\text{BIC} = -2\log L + p\log NaBIC=−2logL+plog(N+224)\text{aBIC} = -2\log L + p\log\left(\frac{N+2}{24}\right)
